note: Attempts held outside the browser. The app merges any entry whose id it has not seen into its own database on load, and commits this file back when anything changes. Ids must be stable and unique — re-merging the same id is a no-op, and changing an id creates a duplicate attempt.

attempts.notes:
Outer loop over rows, inner loop over stars, println outside the inner loop. n = 0 needs no special case: the outer condition is false on the first check, so nothing prints.

Total stars = 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2.
Time O(n^2). Space O(1) — printed output is not memory the method allocated.

Accepted on LeetCode. The else-if chain is doing the real work: i % 15 is tested before i % 3, so 15 is claimed by "FizzBuzz" rather than "Fizz". i % 15 is a valid combined test because 3 and 5 are coprime.

Time O(n). Space O(n) — unlike the star triangle the output is the return value, so it counts.

Also studied a lazy AbstractList variant that stores nothing and computes each element in get(index): O(1) to create and O(1) held, but it recomputes on every access. Recorded in solutions/01-logic/FizzBuzz.java.

Read the last digit with q % 10, add it, drop it with q / 10, stop when q hits zero. Math.abs covers negatives and n = 0 falls out for free because the condition is false before the first pass.

Time O(log n) with respect to the input value n, which is the same statement as "linear in the number of digits" — digits in n = floor(log10(n)) + 1. n going from 9 to 1000000 is a factor of over 100000, while the work goes from 1 turn to 7: buying one more iteration costs multiplying n by ten. Space O(1) — three ints regardless of how large n is.

The tell: a loop that divides its variable by a constant each pass is logarithmic.

Slips: first version added q instead of the extracted digit p, and a second version declared p twice (method scope and loop scope), which does not compile.

Solved with the bonus version - overflow checked before the multiply, no long anywhere.

t = t * 10 + mod rebuilds the number. No Math.abs: Java's remainder takes the sign of the dividend, so -123 % 10 is -3 and negatives fall out with no special case, which also sidesteps the Integer.MIN_VALUE negation trap. Trailing zeros need no special case either - leading zeros simply have no representation in an int.

The guard is t > MAX/10 || t < MIN/10, checked before multiplying. It omits the usual boundary clause (t == MAX/10 && mod > 7) and is still correct for int, because reaching t == 214748364 requires the input to end in 463847412, so the remaining leading digit would have to make n at least 8463847412 - far outside int. Every 10-digit int starts with 1 or 2. Verified against a long-based reference over 347 million values with zero mismatches.

Time O(log n) in the input value, equivalently linear in the digit count. Space O(1) - two ints regardless of n. Same as the previous problem; rebuilding a number instead of summing changed the arithmetic, not the cost.

Guard n < 2 before the loop so 1, 0 and negatives are rejected without entering it, then trial division up to the square root with i <= Math.sqrt(n). The <= matters: 9 and 25 are only caught because i is allowed to reach the root exactly.

Using Math.sqrt rather than i * i also avoids the overflow that breaks the i * i form near MAX_VALUE, where 46341 squared wraps negative and the loop runs past its stopping point. Measured: the sqrt form answers 2147483647 in 2.6 ms; the i * i form answers it wrongly after 12.5 seconds. Calling Math.sqrt inside the condition costs nothing, since n never changes and the JIT hoists it.

Time O(sqrt n), not O(n) - that was the initial answer and it was wrong. Brute force trial division to n-1 is the O(n) version. The bound holds because if n = a * b with a the smaller factor then a cannot exceed sqrt(n), so a composite must reveal a factor at or below its root. Space O(1).

Verified against a reference over 3 million values with zero disagreements.
